summary.text: The received pictographic account relates 了 to 子, describing it as 子 without arms; later commentary interprets it as crossed or entangled legs. The graph also writes “finish,” but the link between that word and the picture is unresolved.

formation.text: The received account treats 了 as a pictograph related to 子, with the arms omitted. A later interpretation sees crossed or entangled legs. These are competing readings of the graph, not confirmed depictions of an early inscription.

history.text: The received account relates the graph to 子; later commentary reads it as crossed or entangled legs. The cited accounts do not establish a securely dated earliest form or a sequence of graphic changes.

uncertainties.text: The character’s use for “finish” has been explained either as sound-based borrowing or through a proposed path from entanglement to tying and completion. The old name and any sound match are unverified, and no dated examples establish the proposed semantic steps.

Accounts trace the completed-action particle to Tang–Song usage, but the cited summaries do not provide dated primary examples. A possible interaction between sentence-final 了 and 也 in some dialects remains tentative.

senses.text: The received entry glosses 了 with 尦; later commentary interprets this as legs crossing or becoming entangled. This is a historical interpretation, not direct confirmation of what an early inscription depicted.

Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed”; a Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the graphic interpretations remain unresolved.

overview.text: In Mandarin, 了 commonly marks a completed action or a change of state. One proposal is that the graph was reused for “finish” because its old name sounded similar, though neither that name nor the match is verified.
